Seersucker (indexers are programs in indexers/) guessed that an agent with only indexers/README.md and some existing code could write an indexer that passes phoropter index --check. Jeff tested it. A fresh agent, given his Roslyn code from glass-blower and the guide, and told never to read phoropter's source, built phoropter-index-roslyn, a syntax-only indexer that passes on a real solution (397 definitions in 0.15s). Then, at Jeff's suggestion, it wrapped scip-dotnet for comparison. It logged every question the guide didn't answer, thirty of them, in its own QUESTIONS.md. That file is the evidence for this plan.

The comparison was decisive. The syntax-only indexer found 338 definitions in 0.2s, on any commit, offline, with nothing restored. scip-dotnet found 251 in 12s with a warm cache, had no definitions for records' positional properties, primary constructors or extension members, collided on namespaces, and failed offline with an empty cache after two minutes of NuGet retries. The roslyn indexer stays where it is, third-party, on PATH. It's the first living proof of that half of the contract.

Decision: The guide says what condition the checkout is in

where indexers/README.md file page

quote `<dir>` is the repository checked out at one commit, at a temporary path. Each

Because (the experiment, #1 and #25): the agent's first question was whether the checkout is restored or built. It isn't, and it may be offline: phoropter checks out a commit, perhaps years old, and runs the indexer on it. The guide says so, and says an indexer that works from source alone is the one that keeps working on old commits. The comparison measured why: the build-based indexer needed the network and gigabytes, and failed without them.

Decision: A package is named by the compiler's name for it, and may not be unique

where indexers/README.md file page

quote `package.json`. For Go, the module path in `go.mod`. For .NET, the project's

Because (the experiment, #22 and #27): "PackageId or AssemblyName" let the two indexers name one package differently, and phoropter asks for a package by name. The guide says AssemblyName for .NET, which is the compiler's name and scip-dotnet's, and readable without loading anything. It also says a package name may name several projects in one repository (copies of ServiceDefaults in four solutions). Then the first in path order answers, and no symbol is ever invented across copies. Inventing them was the real bug the comparison caught.

Decision: Name things as your language's SCIP indexer does, except where it loses information

where indexers/README.md file page

quote Leave out local variables. A plan anchors what a reader can find by name. Every type,

Because (the experiment, #3, #4, #12, #24): following an established indexer's naming answered constructors, indexers, operators and events. Following it blindly would have copied its losses: scip-dotnet keeps only the innermost namespace segment, so same-named types collide, and it doesn't encode generic arity, so Foo and Foo<T> collide. The guide says to follow the established naming, except that full namespace paths are kept and arity is written when a name is reused (Foo#, then the CLR's `Foo`1`#). It also covers partial types (one definition, the first part in path order) and what's optional: parameters and type parameters, better left out.

Decision: The output's edges are said plainly

where indexers/README.md file page

quote - **`missing`:** packages named on the command line that you couldn't find. Phoropter

Because (the experiment, #10, #26, #29): missing means any package the indexer knows of but couldn't index, whether or not it was named, so a project that failed to load never looks absent. It may be omitted when empty. Definitions come only from files in the checkout: generated files in obj/ and source-generator output aren't definitions, since no plan can quote them.

Decision: Phoropter stops an indexer that runs too long

where src/indexers.ts file page

quote const r = spawnSync(info.command[0], [...info.command.slice(1), dir, ...packages], { cwd: info.cwd, encoding: 'utf8', maxBuffer: 1 << 30 });

Because (the experiment, #30): phoropter runs an indexer with no time limit, so a NuGet retry loop would stall a whole build. After a limit, phoropter stops it, and its anchors show no-index, saying it timed out. The guide says what an indexer can expect: a time limit, and no promise of the network. The limit is 5 minutes (Jeff), with PHOROPTER_INDEX_TIMEOUT (in seconds) to change it. The syntax-only indexer takes a fraction of a second, a build-based one around a minute on a fresh machine, and anything past five minutes is more likely stuck than slow. Two and ten minutes were weighed.

Decision: phoropter symbols groups its output by scheme

where src/cli.ts file page

quote const candidates = indexers().filter((i) => i.extensions.includes(ext));

Because (the experiment, #23): with two indexers claiming .cs, their symbols came out interleaved. Anchors were never ambiguous, since a symbol's scheme picks its indexer, but a plan author reading the list couldn't tell them apart at a glance. Output is grouped under a heading per scheme, and --scheme picks one. A per-repository preference would be configuration, which waits for a need.

Decline: Bringing the roslyn indexer into indexers/dotnet/

Because (Claude, not asked): it's the only indexer found on PATH, written outside this repository from the guide alone. Moving it in would leave that half of the contract with no living example. It can move in later, if keeping it outside stops being worth that.
